137: “Well, well,” she said, “I am no accountant. Let us hurry away, hurry away.” And she waved the paper aside. “Neither upon that accursed zero, however, nor upon that equally accursed red do I mean to stake a cent,” I muttered to myself as I entered the Casino.
135: Of what the ultimate calculations consisted I do not exactly remember, but at all events they were alarming. Receiving twelve thousand florins in gold, I took also the statement of accounts, and carried it out to the Grandmother.
133: “The clerk says that others will give you even less than he.”
131: “Pray recollect yourself!” cried the old lady. “And may my money choke you! Alexis Ivanovitch, tell him that we can easily repair to someone else.”
129: “Yes, one of the clerks. The thieves!”
128: “Would one of the clerks do, Madame?”
126: “The thieves!” she exclaimed as she clapped her hands together. “Never mind, though. Get the documents cashed—No; send the banker out to me,” she added as an afterthought.
123: The process of changing involved complicated calculations which soon necessitated my return to the Grandmother for instructions.
121: I entered to get the securities changed, while the Grandmother remained outside in the porch, and the rest waited at a little distance, in doubt as to their best course of action. At length the old lady turned such an angry stare upon them that they departed along the road towards the Casino.
119: “Here we are, Madame,” I announced. “Here is the moneychanger’s office.”
117: “Have done with you and your milk!” cried the old lady. “Go and stuff yourself as much as you like, but my stomach simply recoils from the idea. What are you stopping for? I have nothing to say to you.”
115: “Du lait, de l’herbe fraiche”—the idyll, the ideal of the Parisian bourgeois—his whole outlook upon “la nature et la verité”!
113: “Nous boirons du lait, sur l’herbe fraiche,” added De Griers with the snarl almost of a wild beast.
112: “Begone with you and your views!” said the Grandmother angrily as she waved him away. “And there are trees there, and we could have tea under them,” continued the General—now in utter despair.
110: “My good mother,” he said as he approached her, “—my good mother, pray let, let—” (his voice was beginning to tremble and sink) “—let us hire a carriage, and go for a drive. Near here there is an enchanting view to be obtained. We-we-we were just coming to invite you to go and see it.”
109: “You had better try and stop her yourself,” I returned—also in a whisper.
107: “Stop her, stop her,” whispered the General in consternation.
105: De Griers stamped his foot with vexation, and hastened to communicate the tidings to the General. Meanwhile we continued to wheel the old lady along.
103: “She has lost this morning’s winnings,” I whispered, “and also twelve thousand gülden of her original money. At the present moment we are going to get some bonds changed.”
102: I dropped behind a little, and immediately was pounced upon by De Griers.
100: “Well, well, well!” exclaimed the Grandmother. “But we have no time to stop. What do you want? I can’t talk to you here.”
98: At the turning from the square into the Avenue we came face to face with the whole of our party—the General, De Griers, Mlle. Blanche, and her mother. Only Polina and Mr. Astley were absent.
94: “Hurry, hurry!” commanded the Grandmother. “Show me the nearest way to the money-changer’s. Is it far?”
90: I wheeled the chair out of the throng, and, the bearers making their appearance, we left the Casino.
88: “Rubbish! I am determined to retrieve my losses. Take me away, and call those fools of bearers.”
86: “Quite so; to any amount you please. But you will lose on the transaction what would frighten even a Jew.”
84: “But there is a money-changer’s office here, is there not? They told me I should be able to get any sort of paper security changed!”
76: “But you have no money with which to do it, Madame. In this satchel I can see only a few five percent bonds and some transfers—no actual cash.”
74: “I see they are,” she replied with, as it were, the calmness of despair. “I see they are,” she muttered again as she gazed straight in front of her, like a person lost in thought. “Ah well, I do not mean to rest until I have staked another four thousand.”
72: I did so, and lost. Again, and yet again, we lost. “Madame, your twelve thousand gülden are now gone,” at length I reported.
70: “You see, you see!” she exclaimed as she nudged me. “Stake another four thousand.”
68: This time we won, and the Grandmother recovered herself a little.
63: “I cannot, Madame. The largest stake allowed is four thousand gülden.”
62: “Stake again, stake again—eight thousand at a stroke!”
59: “Never mind. I cannot rest until I have won back my losses. Stake!”
57: “But,” I whispered, “such a quantity of money—”
55: “Very well. Stake another four thousand gülden upon the red. Take this banknote to do it with. I have still got twenty thousand roubles in actual cash.”
54: “I cannot take it upon myself to advise you, for you will only blame me if I do so. Play at your own discretion. Say exactly what you wish staked, and I will stake it.”
52: “No—stay,” she put in hastily. “Where are you going to? Why should you leave me? You fool! No, no... stay here. It is I who was the fool. Tell me what I ought to do.”
50: “Farewell, then, Madame.” And I turned to depart.
49: “You and your mischances!” she whispered threateningly. “Go! Away at once!”
47: “But, Madame, I only explained the game to you. How am I to answer for every mischance which may occur in it?”
45: “To think that that accursed zero should have turned up now! ” she sobbed. “The accursed, accursed thing! And, it is all your fault,” she added, rounding upon me in a frenzy. “It was you who persuaded me to cease staking upon it.”
41: The wheel revolved while the Grandmother sat as bolt upright, and with as proud and quiet a mien, as though she had not the least doubt of winning.
39: “But, Madame, that will be so much to venture!” I remonstrated. “Suppose the red should not turn up?” The Grandmother almost struck me in her excitement. Her agitation was rapidly making her quarrelsome. Consequently, there was nothing for it but to stake the whole four thousand gülden as she had directed.
37: “To the devil with that zero!” she exclaimed. “Stake four thousand gülden upon the red.”
36: By the fifth round, however, the Grandmother was weary of the scheme.
34: “But you see, you see,” whispered the old lady. “We have now recovered almost all that we staked. Try zero again. Let us do so another ten times, and then leave off.”
31: The red turned up, but zero missed again, and we only got our thousand gülden back.
29: “Never mind,” she interrupted. “Keep on staking upon zero, and also stake a thousand gülden upon rouge. Here is a banknote with which to do so.”
27: “We have lost 144 ten-gülden pieces,” I replied. “I tell you, Madame, that zero may not turn up until nightfall.”
23: “How many times have we lost?” she inquired—actually grinding her teeth in her excitement.
21: “Stake again,” said the old lady with an impatient nudge of my elbow, and I obeyed.
19: As soon as ever we arrived the Grandmother ordered me to stake twelve ten-gülden pieces in succession upon zero. Once, twice, and thrice I did so, yet zero never turned up.
14: At the Casino the Grandmother seemed to be expected, for no time was lost in procuring her former place beside the croupier. It is my opinion that though croupiers seem such ordinary, humdrum officials—men who care nothing whether the bank wins or loses—they are, in reality, anything but indifferent to the bank’s losing, and are given instructions to attract players, and to keep a watch over the bank’s interests; as also, that for such services, these officials are awarded prizes and premiums. At all events, the croupiers of Roulettenberg seemed to look upon the Grandmother as their lawful prey—whereafter there befell what our party had foretold.
12: “Why have you attached yourselves to the party? We are not going to take you with us every time. Go home at once.” Then, when the servants had pulled hasty bows and departed, she added to me: “You are all the escort I need.”
10: “Lift me up,” she cried to the bearers, and once more we set out for the roulette-salons.
8: True enough, I found Madame in the hotel verandah—much put about at my delay, for she had been unable to contain herself until four o’clock.
5: “My mistress was unable to sleep,” explained Potapitch; “so, after tossing about for a while, she suddenly rose, called for her chair, and sent me to look for you. She is now in the verandah.”
2: At this moment three low, respectful knocks sounded at the door; which, on being opened, revealed a chambermaid, with Potapitch behind her—come from the Grandmother to request that I should attend her in her rooms. “She is in a bad humour,” added Potapitch.
0: “Alexis Ivanovitch,” he began, “pray pardon me for having said what I did just now—for having said more than I meant to do. I beg and beseech you, I kiss the hem of your garment, as our Russian saying has it, for you, and only you, can save us. I and Mlle. de Cominges, we all of us beg of you—But you understand, do you not? Surely you understand?” and with his eyes he indicated Mlle. Blanche. Truly he was cutting a pitiful figure!
